item.title: When Animals Were Put on Trial in Medieval Europe
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with pictures of the animals it comes from, sometimes dressed in chef’s garb and cheerfully serving up the very dishes they’re about to become.) Things were different in medieval Europe, where animals were both a necessity and a potential danger. History records many instances of serious harm done to humans by horses, bulls, and especially pigs, who seem to have had a particular tendency to turn on children.

Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhuman act, a term that, in these cases, applies more than figuratively. As for the fate of the violently offending animal, we might imagine that it would be summarily slaughtered, but between the tenth and eighteenth centuries — and especially in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — it might well have been brought into a courtroom first. Though other creatures had already been subject to legal proceedings for quite some time, “the earliest recorded pig trial took place in Fontenay-aux-Roses, just outside Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexander Lee at History Today. “By the early fifteenth century, however, they had become established practice throughout Normandy and the Île-de-France,” eventually spreading beyond the border to Italy, Germany, and the Low Countries.

“As contemporary students of the Corpus iuris civilis knew, it was a basic principle of Roman law that animals could not be culpable,” Lee adds. “Lacking reason, they were incapable of harboring criminal intent and hence could not be guilty of a crime.” But in un-Roman northern France, “the administration of secular justice was still largely the concern of local seigneurs and was governed predominantly by custom rather than statute.” Thus sustained, animal trials served purposes beyond simple punishment. “For medieval people, the world was created by God in a very logical way, with animals created first, in order to serve and help human beings who were created in the image of God,” says University of Liverpool medieval European monster expert Damian Kempf, quoted in Popular Science by Anne Ewbank. In that worldview, trying and executing a pig could “restore what was broken.”

Unlike domestic animals, according to Sonya Vatomsky at JSTOR Daily, destructive mice, beetles, snails, weevils, and other vermin would be sent to ecclesiastical tribunals. “Despite being unlikely candidates for Catholicism, such creatures were punished with excommunication, not execution,” she writes, since casting them out of God’s domain would allow humans to exterminate them with peace of mind. Vatomsky also quotes economist Peter T. Leeson’s theory that the Catholic Church tried more animals when people got lax about tithing, with the aim of “bolstering citizens’ belief in the validity of Church punishments for tithe evasion.” Putting animals on trial may now strike us as grotesque, but like any alien-seeming episode of history, it also reveals the beliefs on which a past society operated — a mode of analysis that gets one wondering how far the modern United States is from giving them the right to sue.

item.title: 2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played During Homer’s Time
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twitter

The prolific Hans Zimmer scored Christopher Nolan’s films over the dozen years from Batman Begins through Dunkirk. From 2020’s Tenet onward, Nolan has employed the younger Swedish composer Ludwig Göransson. Just what difference this has made in the resulting pictures is a matter best left to the scrutiny of the most obsessive fans, but any viewer can hear how much Zimmer and Göransson differ stylistically. This past summer, the siren song included on the soundtrack of The Odyssey featured one of the latter’s particularly notable choices: the use of an aulos, a double-reeded wind instrument much played back in ancient Greece.

Though Göransson didn’t have a genuinely ancient aulos on hand, of course, the sound produced by the replica proved evocative enough. But just this year, as it happens, a bone flute actually dating from the period in which Homer wrote The Odyssey was unearthed from the archaeological site of ancient Troy in modern-day northwestern Turkey.

As Smithsonian.com’s Meilan Solly writes, the past 160 years of digging there have produced “a pair of gold diadems, more than 100 two-handled wine goblets, and arrowheads and weapons dated to the Late Bronze Age, among other artifacts.” This 2,800-year-old flute isn’t just the first musical instrument discovered at the site, but also further evidence that Troy wasn’t the ghost town it was once assumed to be in the eighth century BC.

As always when dealing with ancient artifacts — and especially ones, as these pictures reveal, in a less-than-whole state — we should be careful with our terms. “Calling the object a flute is the excavators’ choice of word, and the type remains open,” says Ancient Origins. While this new discovery could potentially be a real Greek aulos, “without hole counts or a published drawing, matching the Troy find to that design is premature.” Archaeologists have unearthed similar instruments elsewhere, dating from different periods, but never before has one emerged from the buried remains of a city so rich in legendary associations. To those in search of a deeper understanding of antiquity, the site continues to sound a siren song of its own.

item.title: Watch Seoul’s 6,500-Year Evolution in a Mesmerizing 3D Animated Time Lapse
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

In this century, few countries have been as visibly successful as South Korea. China’s vertiginous economic rise once absorbed vast amounts of news-media attention, but its soft power has comparatively little reach across the wider world, at least in English-speaking countries. By this point, many if not most Westerners haven’t just eaten Korean food, but also driven a Korean car, heard Korean pop music, or watched a Korean film or TV show. The resulting sense of familiarity can prove deceptive to those who eventually make the trip there, but it does, at least, mark an improvement on the scant knowledge of the place they had before. Not so long ago, they could say little with certainty except this: South Korea’s got Seoul.

I first saw that pun on a T‑shirt in high school, long before I knew much of anything about Korea myself. Now, having lived there for more than a decade, I’ve been able to watch from the inside as the country’s capital has become an unlikely object of general interest. As evidence, take the 1.2 million views already racked up by the new video from Latos Charts above, a 3D animated time lapse showing the evolution of Seoul over six and a half often tumultuous millennia.

It reveals, among other things, that the city didn’t exist for most of the history of Korean civilization — but then, neither did the country. The postwar division of the peninsula into North and South has a kind of precedent in the warring kingdoms that occupied it before its unification by a series of states culminating in the 500-year rule of the Joseon Dynasty.

If you’ve watched one of the many popular historical “K‑dramas,” Joseon was most likely its period setting. Now generally regarded as the predecessor of modern-day Korea, it passes in two minutes of the time lapse, during which Seoul, then known as Hanyang, takes amid its geomantically protective mountains more or less the shape it has today, at least north of the Han River. In fact, up until the seventies, there was no city to speak of south of the Han: the development of the more recently musically satirized Gangnam, literally “south of the river,” was part of the top-down push for economic development — in effect, hitting the fast-forward button on history — that followed the devastation of the Korean War. That chapter of history comes around eight minutes into the video, after which lookalike high-rise complexes start popping up like mushrooms after a monsoon.

However comfortable a lifestyle they’ve offered to middle-class Seoulites, the sight of those apateu danji unsettles some Western observers, who encounter them in photographs meant to depict the city as a kind of futuristic dystopia. They exaggerate, of course, but even someone who appreciates Seoul as much as I do has to admit that, alongside its impressive qualities — the magnificent subway system, for example, extolled in the Not Just Bikes video above — the city has its problems, as does the nation for which it stands. Understanding it in all its complexity requires first (even before learning the Korean language) grasping its sheer centrality, greater than Tokyo’s to Japan or even Paris’ to France. To a great extent, South Korea hasn’t just got Seoul, it is Seoul. And maybe, if its prominence in the wider world continues to grow, the punning will eventually stop. In Korean history, stranger things have certainly happened.

item.title: Why Do We Say We “Barked” Our Shins?
item.description:

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

After Diana from Williamsburg, Virginia, scraped the front of her leg on a chair, she fretted to her grown daughters she had barked her shin. Neither daughter had ever heard the expression. This kind of bark refers not to what a dog does, but to removing, peeling back, or scraping, just like stripping bark from a tree. Ouch! The phrase goes back at least to the early 1810s. This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of “Why Do We Say We “Barked” Our Shin?”

You have A Way with Words.

My name is Diana Stafford, and I’m in Williamsburg, Virginia.

Oh, well, it’s nice to talk with you.

Several weeks ago, I scraped my leg against a chair, and just the very front part of my leg.

And when my daughters asked me what had happened, I said, I barked my shin.

And these are two daughters who are well educated and well read, They both said, I’ve never heard that expression before.

So I thought maybe you people would help me figure out where that came from.

Oh, and how old are they that they didn’t know the expression?

They’re both in their fifties.

Fifties.

Shin.

Yeah.

You know, I never used it growing up.

I only learned it when I started working with language much much later.

Yeah.

It’s got a…

It’s not quite archaic, I wouldn’t say, but it’s certainly a little fossilized.

‘ Cause what’s happening here is we don’t really use barked that way very often.

And this is the verb bark, meaning to remove or peel back or to scrape something like you might do with the actual bark of a tree, which is what it’s referring to.

So, barking something may mean taking the bark off of it and that’s kind of what you’re doing if you injure yourself enough to peel back the skin.

And then shin, of course, is just another name for a particular body part down there at the lower leg.

It’s got all these things that are terrible about living in Brooklyn, New York.

Ouch.

Right?

item.title: Inspiration from Charles Bukowski: You Might Be Old, Your Life May Be “Crappy,” But You Can Still Make Good Art
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, cultural context

Now more than ever, there’s tremendous pressure to make it big while you’re young.

Pity the 31-year-old who fails to make it onto a 30-under-30 list…

The soon-to-graduate high schooler passed over for YouTube stardom…

The great hordes who creep into middle age without so much as a TED Talk to their names…

Social media definitely magnifies the sensation that an unacceptable number of our peers have been granted first-class cabins aboard a ship that’s sailed without us. If we weren’t so demoralized, we’d sue Instagram for creating the impression that everyone else’s perfectly filtered life is leading to book deals and profiles in The New Yorker.

Don’t despair, dear reader. Charles Bukowski is about to make your day from beyond the grave.

In 1993, at the age of 73, the late writer and self-described “spoiled old toad,” took a break from recording the audiobook of Run With the Hunted to reflect upon his “crappy” life.

Some of these thoughts made it into Drew Christie’s animation, above, a reminder that the smoothest road isn’t always necessarily the richest one.

In service of his ill-paying muse, Bukowski logged decades in unglamorous jobs—dishwasher, truck driver and loader, gas station attendant, stock boy, warehouseman, shipping clerk, parking lot attendant, Red Cross orderly, elevator operator, and most notoriously, postal carrier and clerk. These gigs gave him plenty of material, the sort of real world experience that eludes those upon whom literary fame and fortune smiles early.

(His alcoholic misadventures provided yet more material, earning him such honorifics as the “poet laureate of L.A. lowlife” and “enfant terrible of the Meat School poets.”)

One might also take comfort in hearing a writer as prodigious as Bukowski revealing that he didn’t hold himself to the sort of daily writing regimen that can be difficult to achieve when one is juggling day jobs, student loans, and/or a family. Also appreciated is the far-from-cursory nod he accords the therapeutic benefits that are available to all those who write, regardless of any public or financial recognition:

Three or four nights out of seven. If I don’t get those in, I don’t act right. I feel sick. I get very depressed. It’s a release. It’s my psychiatrist, letting this shit out. I’m lucky I get paid for it. I’d do it for nothing. In fact, I’d pay to do it. Here, I’ll give you ten thousand a year if you’ll let me write.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

item.title: “Just Deserts” or “Just Desserts”?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

Is it just desserts or just deserts? This particular desert isn’t an arid place, however. This desert is an old noun coming from French, which means “something deserved.” The after-dinner dessert, on the other hand, is from an entirely different French word meaning “to clear the table,” which is what happens before those last sweet treats are set out. This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of ““Just Deserts” or “Just Desserts”?”

Gina Bradshaw from Harvest Alabama emailed us with a question.

I’ve heard the phrase just dessert many times, and in my mind, I thought it was spelled d e s s e r t, as in someone getting the dessert or treat they deserved good or bad.

But I recently read the phrase and noticed it was spelled d e s e r t, like an arid place with little precipitation.

Have I been mentally spelling this wrong my whole life?

Well, Gina can relax and not worry about it because that is an incredibly common confusion.

A lot of people aren’t quite sure what that dessert is in there in the middle.

Is it the food?

Is it a dry place?

Is it something else?

It is what you deserve.

It’s…

Yeah.

The word des…

Dessert is a very old noun that means something deserved.

It comes from French, from a French word that means to deserve.

So when we have our just desserts, we…

If there is justice in the world, we are getting what we deserve.

So it’s a third word, a third dessert.

That’s right.

And the dessert that means what you have after dinner comes from a different French word that means to clear the table.

Oh, like to deservice, basically, take everything off.

Because that’s what you traditionally would do in a more, you know, sophisticated meal environment.

You take off the main plates and maybe bring out the cognac and some sweets at the end.

Right.

Right.

So it’s a very understandable confusion.

But…

Yeah.

Just Desserts has one s in the middle.

English is confusing, but it is a heck of a lot of fun to sort out.

And that’s what Martha and I are here for, not just English, but any language you wanna toss at us.

We’ll give it a go.

item.title: “Pony” as a Study Aid, From 19th-Century British Translations to Maritime Academy Tests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, historical context

Joe from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, asks about pony, the term he and his fellow maritime academy students used to mean “a practice test” or “a copy of a previous test” to help them crib for an exam. Among 19th-century British students, the slang term pony meant “a translation or summary used as a study shortcut,” also known as a horse or trot. Linguist Connie Eble notes that the same concept has been modernized in North Carolina college slang as automobile and bicycle—something that, in other words, allows a student to coast through an exam. A listener who graduated from a merchant marine engineering school in the early 1980s emailed to say he remembers that when he was a student, a pony was “a copy of a test from previous classes,” and savvy instructors sometimes changed tiny details from year to year to thwart cheaters. This is part of a complete episode.

Transcript of ““Pony” as a Study Aid: From 19th-Century British Translations to Maritime Academy Old Tests”

You have A Way with Words.

Hi.

I’m Joe, and I’m calling from Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

Hi, Joe.

Welcome to the program.

And we use pony to describe a practice test or if you had, like, an old copy of a test from a year prior, you’d say, oh, did you study the pony?

That’s so interesting.

A pony was a literal translation or a summary of a text that was used as a shortcut or or a study aid, you know, something that you could use to to crib.
